newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bank gold sales fail to rattle market.
newsitem.headline: Australian bank gold sales fail to rattle market.

text.p: The gold market has reacted with little fanfare to the latest central bank gold sales, 167 tonnes by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), owing to big short positions in the market, bullion dealers said.
Spot gold was fetching US$332.30-$332.60 an ounce at 1445 GMT (12.45 a.m.), little changed on the previous day's price.
But the sales are likely to eventually weigh on gold prices worldwide, they said.
"I think that the Reserve Bank has gone out and sold 167 tonnes of our second biggest export is very negative for gold and for the Aussie (Australian dollar)," a Sydney dealer said.

Gold already suffers an image problem: it is longer seen so much as a monetary symbol but just another commodity, like rubber or corn, or more on the mark, silver, now more closely sought as an industrial metal.
This is being reflected in the current gold price, the lowest in more than four years.
Because of large short positions in the market, the near-term impact of the sales might actually lift prices as more gold is seen injected into the market, some dealers believe.
But longer term it is more likely to represent the latest no-vote of confidence for gold.

Over the last five years central bank gold sales from Belgium, Canada the Netherlands, South Africa and elsewhere have done little to polish gold's image and there is little to suggest the RBA sales will be any different.
If gold does become totally demonetised, its change of state could happen more quickly than silver's in the 19th century.

But the impact of the RBA sales will be felt hardest at home, where Australia's gold mining industry has been struggling against low international prices made worse by a stong Australian-to U.S. dollar exchange rate.
Making it worse, miners have to dig deeper to find the same amount of gold, raising operating costs.

The RBA said on Friday that over the past six months it had sold 167 tonnes of gold, more than half the nation's annual output, in favour of securites denominated in U.S. dollars, German marks and Japanese yen.
The RBA said it reckoned the securities were a better investment, given Australia's vast in-ground reserves of gold.
But for many of Australia's gold miners, already on the verge of collapse, the timing is terrible.

It is estimated some 10 percent of the Australian gold miners are unable to mine gold under A$480 an ounce, on a cash cost basis. This means that excluding forward sales at higher prices, the miners are oprating at a loss.
Gold on Wednesday was fetching only A$441 an ounce.

Melbourne-based consultants Surbiton Associates Pty Ltd calculate the weighted average cash cost for operations representing 82 percent of all Australian primary gold production was A$376 an ounce in the last quarter.
Using such data, and taking into account other costs, such as amortisation, depreciation and financing, there is little margin at the current price, Sandra Close of Surbiton said.
Australia produces nearly 300 tonnes of gold a year, making it the world's third largest gold producing country.

If gold prices fall much further, some analysts think Australian gold miners may be ripe for takeover by foreign companies who may perceive the mines as undervalued due to a cyclical low period in the gold price.
-- Melbourne newsroom 61-3 9286-1421
